from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

class Section1Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Inscribed Square Problem", [
            "Can we inscribe a square in any closed loop?",
            "Consider a smooth, continuous, non-self-intersecting curve.",
            "Even for irregular loops, a square often exists."
        ])
        
        # Create a circle
        curve = Circle(radius=1.5, color="#FFFFFF")
        self.place_at_grid(curve, 'C3')
        
        # Create quadrilateral vertices tracker
        # Angles: 0, 90, 180, 270 degrees
        angles = [0, PI/2, PI, 3*PI/2]
        dots = VGroup(*[Dot(color="#FF0000") for _ in range(4)])
        
        def update_dots(d):
            t = self.time
            for i, dot in enumerate(dots):
                angle = angles[i] + t
                dot.move_to(curve.get_center() + 1.5 * np.array([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle), 0]))
        
        quad = VMobject(color="#FF0000")
        quad.add_updater(lambda m: m.set_points_smoothly([d.get_center() for d in dots] + [dots[0].get_center()]))
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(curve))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.add(dots, quad)
        dots.add_updater(update_dots)
        self.wait(2)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.lecture[0].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FFFF00")
        self.wait(3)

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.lecture[1].set_color(WHITE)
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#00FF00")
        
        # Change quad color to indicate square condition
        quad.set_color("#00FF00")
        for dot in dots:
            dot.set_color("#00FF00")
            
        self.wait(3)
        dots.remove_updater(update_dots)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "Borsuk-Ulam theorem is our logical bridge.",
            "It links sphere points to plane values.",
            "It proves existence by mapping to zero.",
            "Symmetry helps us identify the square's corners.",
            "This confirms a square must always exist."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Mathematical Core: Symmetry and the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem", lecture_lines)

        # Visual elements
        torus = Torus(major_radius=1.5, minor_radius=0.5, resolution=(24, 24)).set_color(WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(torus, 'C3', scale_factor=0.8)

        antipodal_1 = Dot(color=RED).move_to(torus.get_center() + np.array([1.5, 0, 0]))
        antipodal_2 = Dot(color=RED).move_to(torus.get_center() - np.array([1.5, 0, 0]))
        
        intersection_point = Dot(color=GREEN).move_to(torus.get_center())

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(torus))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFF00")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(Rotate(torus, angle=PI/2), FadeIn(antipodal_1), FadeIn(antipodal_2))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#00FFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(antipodal_1.animate.move_to(torus.get_center()), antipodal_2.animate.move_to(torus.get_center()))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF00FF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        self.play(FadeOut(antipodal_1), FadeOut(antipodal_2))
        self.lecture[3].set_color("#FFA500")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(intersection_point))
        self.lecture[4].set_color("#00FF00")
        self.wait(1)

class Section5Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Application & Conclusion", [
            "Toeplitz's Conjecture remains open for general curves.",
            "Topology provides certainty beyond simple trial-error.",
            "Mathematics guarantees success for these shapes."
        ])
        
        # Create a complex loop and a square
        points = [
            [-1.5, 1, 0], [0, 1.5, 0], [1.5, 1, 0], 
            [1.5, -1, 0], [0.5, -1.5, 0], [-1.5, -0.5, 0]
        ]
        loop = VMobject(color=WHITE).set_points_smoothly(points + [points[0]])
        square = Square(side_length=1.5, color=WHITE)
        
        self.place_in_area(loop, "B2", "E5")
        self.place_in_area(square, "C3", "D4")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(Create(loop), FadeIn(square))
        self.lecture[0].set_color("#FFFFFF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        self.play(square.animate.scale(0.8).rotate(PI/6))
        self.lecture[1].set_color("#FF00FF")

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        self.play(Flash(square, color="#FF00FF"))
        self.lecture[2].set_color("#FF00FF")
        self.wait(2)

outline.topic: The Toeplitz's Conjecture: Can we always inscribe a square in any closed loop?

sections.title: The Visual Hook: The Inscribed Square Problem
sections.content: Introduce the geometric puzzle: Given a closed continuous curve (like an ink splatter or a rubber band), can we always find four points on the curve that form the vertices of a square? Define the problem visually using a smooth, non-self-intersecting loop.
sections.example: Visualize a cartoon character drawing a 'doodle' on a piece of paper; demonstrate how we can always find a square inside a simple circle, but ask if this holds for a 'wobbly' irregular shape.

sections.title: Prerequisite: The Concept of Configuration Spaces
sections.content: Explain that to solve this, we don't just look at the curve, but at the space of all possible pairs of points on the curve. Introduce the 'Configuration Space' as a 2D surface (a torus or triangle) representing all pairs (x, y) on the curve.
sections.example: Use a grid animation where the x-axis represents the position of the first point and the y-axis represents the second; points on the curve are mapped to coordinates on this grid.

sections.title: Mathematical Core: Symmetry and the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem
sections.content: Introduce the Borsuk-Ulam Theorem as the 'logical bridge.' Explain that for any continuous function from a sphere to a plane, there exist antipodal points that map to the same value. We apply this to the symmetry of squares to prove existence.
sections.example: Show a visual of a sphere and its antipodal points; demonstrate how the 'square' constraint acts as a function that must 'hit zero' (find a perfect square) at some point on the curve.

sections.title: The Proof Logic: Connecting Vertices
sections.content: Explain the construction of the 'square function.' If we pick two points on the curve, the midpoint and the distance between them define a potential square. We show that the space of 'non-square' configurations is inconsistent, implying a square must exist.
sections.example: An animation of a rotating square 'sweeping' through an irregular shape until it snaps perfectly onto four points on the perimeter.

sections.title: Application & Conclusion
sections.content: Summarize that while the theorem holds for 'smooth' loops, it remains an open question for arbitrary non-smooth curves (Toeplitz's Conjecture). Discuss why topology provides certainty where geometric trial-and-error fails.
sections.example: Final shot: A robot arm trying to find a square on an irregular wire loop; the math guarantees the arm will always succeed.
